courses.title: Medical Instrumentation and Biosensors
courses.description: Measurement systems, transducers and biosensors, bioelectric potentials and electrodes, amplifiers, and common patient monitoring instruments.

topics.title: Measurement Systems and Performance
topics.summary: Components of a measurement system and static and dynamic characteristics.

material.heading: Generalised measurement system
material.body: A medical instrument consists of the measurand (the physiological quantity — pressure, flow, temperature, biopotential), a sensor/transducer (converts the measurand into an electrical signal), signal conditioning (amplification, filtering, analogue-to-digital conversion), output display or recording, and often data storage, transmission, alarms and control/feedback. Physiological signals are usually small (µV–mV), noisy and variable, and measurement must not harm the patient or alter the variable being measured.
keyPoints: Measurement must be safe and non-disturbing

material.heading: Performance characteristics
material.body: Static characteristics: accuracy (closeness to the true value), precision (repeatability), resolution (smallest detectable change), sensitivity (output change per input change), linearity, range, zero and sensitivity drift, and hysteresis. Dynamic characteristics describe response to changing inputs: frequency response and bandwidth, time constant, rise time and damping. For example, invasive blood pressure systems need adequate natural frequency and optimal damping (about 0.64) to reproduce the arterial waveform without overshoot (underdamping) or blunting (overdamping). Calibration against standards keeps instruments accurate.

questions.explanation: Calibration maintains accuracy.

questions.explanation: ECG is about 1 mV; EEG tens of µV.

topics.title: Transducers and Biosensors
topics.summary: Resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, thermal and optical transducers, and biosensors such as glucose sensors.

material.heading: Transducer types
material.body: Resistive transducers: strain gauges (resistance changes with deformation — used in pressure transducers, often in a Wheatstone bridge) and thermistors (resistance changes strongly with temperature; NTC thermistors in patient temperature probes). Thermocouples generate a voltage from junctions of dissimilar metals (Seebeck effect). Capacitive transducers sense displacement/pressure. Piezoelectric crystals generate charge when deformed and vibrate when voltage is applied — used in ultrasound transducers and some pulse sensors. Optical sensors (photodiodes, LEDs) are used in pulse oximetry and photoplethysmography. Infrared thermometers detect emitted thermal radiation (tympanic and forehead thermometers).

material.heading: Biosensors
material.body: A biosensor combines a biological recognition element (enzyme, antibody, nucleic acid, cell) with a transducer. The classic example is the electrochemical glucose sensor: glucose oxidase catalyses glucose oxidation, and the resulting current (amperometric measurement) is proportional to glucose concentration — used in glucometers and continuous glucose monitors (CGMs, which measure interstitial fluid glucose). Other biosensors include lateral-flow immunoassays (rapid diagnostic tests for malaria, HIV and pregnancy), ion-selective electrodes, and oxygen (Clark) electrodes. Point-of-care testing brings diagnosis closer to patients.

topics.title: Bioelectric Signals and Electrodes
topics.summary: Origins of biopotentials, ECG, EEG and EMG characteristics, and electrode types and artefacts.

material.heading: Biopotentials
material.body: Excitable cells generate action potentials whose summed activity is recorded at the body surface. Typical signals: ECG (electrocardiogram) about 0.5–4 mV, bandwidth roughly 0.05–150 Hz for diagnostic recordings; EEG (electroencephalogram) about 10–100 µV, 0.5–40 Hz (delta, theta, alpha, beta rhythms); EMG (electromyogram) about 0.1–5 mV, 20–500 Hz or more; EOG (eye movements). The standard 12-lead ECG uses limb leads (I, II, III), augmented limb leads (aVR, aVL, aVF) and six precordial leads (V1–V6); Einthoven's triangle relates the limb leads.
keyPoints: ECG ~1 mV; EEG ~10–100 µV; EMG up to mV
EEG rhythms: delta, theta, alpha, beta
12-lead ECG: I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF, V1–V6

material.heading: Electrodes and artefacts
material.body: Silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) electrodes with conductive gel are standard for surface biopotential recording because they are non-polarisable (low, stable half-cell potential and noise). Skin preparation (cleaning, light abrasion) reduces skin impedance. Other electrodes: needle electrodes (EMG), microelectrodes (single cells), and dry electrodes (wearables). Common artefacts: 50 Hz mains interference (reduced by good grounding, shielding and differential amplifiers with high common-mode rejection, plus notch filters), baseline wander (respiration, movement — high-pass filtering), muscle (EMG) artefact, and loose electrodes.
keyPoints: 50 Hz interference: shielding, CMRR, notch filter

questions.explanation: Removing the stratum corneum improves contact.

topics.title: Biomedical Amplifiers and Signal Conditioning
topics.summary: Operational amplifiers, instrumentation amplifiers, filters, isolation and analogue-to-digital conversion.

material.heading: Amplifiers
material.body: Operational amplifiers (op-amps) have very high gain and input impedance and are configured with feedback as inverting amplifiers (gain = −Rf/Rin), non-inverting amplifiers (gain = 1 + Rf/Rin), voltage followers (buffers), integrators and differentiators. Biopotential amplifiers must have very high input impedance (much greater than electrode–skin impedance), high common-mode rejection ratio (CMRR, often > 100 dB) to reject interference, low noise, appropriate gain (ECG ~1,000) and bandwidth, and protection against defibrillator pulses. The instrumentation amplifier (three op-amps) is the standard differential front end. Isolation amplifiers (optical, transformer or capacitive coupling) separate the patient from mains-connected circuits for safety.

material.heading: Filtering and digitisation
material.body: Filters shape the signal: low-pass (remove high-frequency noise), high-pass (remove drift), band-pass and notch (band-stop, e.g. 50 Hz) filters; active filters use op-amps. Analogue-to-digital converters (ADCs) sample the signal; the Nyquist theorem requires a sampling rate at least twice the highest frequency present, otherwise aliasing occurs — an anti-aliasing low-pass filter precedes the ADC. Resolution depends on bit depth: an n-bit ADC has 2ⁿ levels (e.g. 12-bit = 4,096). Digital signal processing then enables storage, analysis (e.g. automated arrhythmia detection) and telemetry.

questions.stem: An inverting amplifier with Rf = 100 kΩ and Rin = 10 kΩ has a gain of:
questions.explanation: Gain = −Rf/Rin = −10.

Biopotential amplifiers need a high common-mode rejection ratio in order to:
options: Reject interference present equally on both inputs
questions.explanation: Mains interference is largely common-mode.

topics.title: Patient Monitoring Instruments
topics.summary: ECG monitors, non-invasive and invasive blood pressure, pulse oximetry, capnography and alarms.

material.heading: Monitors
material.body: Bedside monitors display ECG, heart rate, non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP — usually oscillometric: the cuff detects pressure oscillations; mean arterial pressure corresponds to maximal oscillation, and systolic/diastolic are derived), invasive blood pressure (arterial line with a fluid-filled catheter, pressure transducer zeroed to atmosphere at the level of the right atrium — phlebostatic axis), temperature, respiratory rate (impedance pneumography) and SpO2. Pulse oximetry uses red (≈ 660 nm) and infrared (≈ 940 nm) light: oxyhaemoglobin absorbs more infrared and deoxyhaemoglobin more red light; the ratio of pulsatile absorbances gives SpO2. Errors: poor perfusion, motion, nail polish, carbon monoxide poisoning (falsely normal SpO2 because carboxyhaemoglobin reads like oxyhaemoglobin), methaemoglobinaemia (tends towards 85%), and skin pigmentation (may overestimate saturation, a recognised equity concern).
keyPoints: Zero invasive transducers at the phlebostatic axis

material.heading: Capnography and alarms
material.body: Capnography measures end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2, normally about 35–45 mmHg) by infrared absorption; the waveform confirms correct endotracheal tube placement (the gold standard — no CO2 trace suggests oesophageal intubation), monitors ventilation and indicates effective CPR. Alarm management: alarms should be set to clinically appropriate limits, prioritised (high/medium/low), and not silenced without checking; excessive false alarms cause 'alarm fatigue'. Central stations and telemetry allow remote monitoring. Regular preventive maintenance and calibration are essential for accuracy.
